papers.title: Determinants and Consequences of Auditors’ Consultations with the National Office
papers.authors: Matthew G. Sherwood, Miguel Minutti-Meza, Aleksandra B. Zimmerman
papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Audit teams may consult with their firm’s national office to obtain specialized expertise, satisfy regulatory and quality control requirements, and demonstrate due professional care. We describe the consultation process based on PCAOB standards, firm methodologies, and auditor interviews. We explain different types of consultations and highlight differences in the determinants and usefulness of mandatory versus voluntary consultations. Using PCAOB inspection data, we show that formal consultations are largely predictable based on engagement characteristics and, on average, are not associated with audit quality. However, two subsets of formal consultations that focus on accounting issues and occur earlier in the engagement process are associated with greater regulatory compliance and higher audit quality. Hence, an increasing reliance on all types of consultations does not automatically translate into higher audit quality. Collectively, our findings deepen our understanding of auditors’ use of national office consultations and their implications for audit practice.
                  Data Availability: Audit engagement data from the PCAOB are proprietary; other data are from public sources.
                  JEL Classification: M4.

papers.title: Could That Happen to Me? Auditor Response When Colleagues Are Named in Lawsuits
papers.authors: Brant E. Christensen, Nathan G. Lundstrom, Nathan J. Newton
papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Litigation risk is an important source of motivation for auditors to conduct high‐quality audits, but theory suggests that certain lawsuits will have a more salient disciplining effect on auditor behavior. To this end, we identify lawsuits naming an individual partner as a co‐defendant along with the audit firm. We then examine how these lawsuits affect subsequent behavior of other auditors in the office of the sued partner. Relative to lawsuits naming only the firm, our results indicate that lawsuits naming individual partners as co‐defendants are significant office‐level events that motivate a meaningful response from non‐sued audit partners in the form of higher quality and fees on existing clients and more careful client portfolio management. These results have practical implications about how auditor litigation incentivizes individual auditors to fulfill their professional duties. For regulators and audit firms seeking to promote audit quality, these findings highlight the disciplining effect of auditors' concern for their personal reputation and litigation exposure. Furthermore, audit committees, clients, and investors may observe elevated audit quality, effort, and fees following partner‐level litigation in the local office.

papers.title: Unintended Regulatory Spillovers: The Impact of Bank Regulatory Oversight on Environmental Enforcement
papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  We explore whether bank regulatory oversight affects the ability of environmental enforcement to reduce industrial emissions. A major objective of environmental enforcement is to reduce industrial emissions by encouraging firms to employ greener production processes and technologies. However, such changes often require external financing obtained from banks, and prior research shows that regulatory oversight of banks can affect bank lending. We find that, on average, the reduction in air pollution in response to county‐level environmental enforcement is attenuated in counties exposed to increased bank regulatory oversight, as measured by severe enforcement actions. Furthermore, we show that the negative impact of bank regulatory oversight on small business lending to affected counties is the likely mechanism behind this on‐average effect. However, when bank regulatory oversight targets banks with stronger capitalization, we find that the negative effect of bank regulatory oversight on environmental enforcement is mitigated. Collectively, our findings suggest that bank regulation has a nuanced effect on the extent to which environmental enforcement reduces emissions, indicating that one regulator's mission can impact the objectives of another.

papers.title:
Would a Balanced
                    <scp>PCAOB</scp>
                    Inspection Approach Increase Auditors' Use of Innovative Audit Procedures?
papers.authors: Yoon Ju Kang, M. David Piercey
papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Prior research criticizes PCAOB inspection reports for focusing solely on audit deficiencies, arguing that this encourages auditors to pursue traditional procedures to demonstrate compliance with standards rather than procedures that maximize audit quality. We contribute to this debate by examining whether the PCAOB's approach discourages auditors from considering innovative audit procedures (that are potentially more effective), since they are, by definition, less standard. We compare the PCAOB's current inspection approach (which focuses on reporting audit deficiencies) to a balanced inspection approach that discloses examples of audit strengths as well as deficiencies discovered during inspections. We predict and find that when the risk of material misstatement (RMM) is moderate, a balanced inspection approach leads auditors to consider the potential effectiveness of innovative audit procedures to a greater extent, ultimately prioritizing more of them in audit plans. Our findings contribute to both research and practice by enhancing our understanding of ways to encourage audit innovation and ultimately improve overall audit quality.

papers.title: Beyond Greenwashing: Environmental Commitments and Gas Flaring in the African Oil Sector
papers.authors: Samuel Chang, Hans B. Christensen, Andrew McKinley
papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Corporations make substantial progress toward their Zero Routine Flaring commitments globally, particularly in Africa where preexisting environmental standards are weak. Moreover, committers’ flaring reductions on the continent are driven primarily by operational improvements rather than offloading assets and are concentrated among committers facing greater stakeholder pressure. Although flaring is higher for assets continuously operated by, awarded to, or divested to noncommitters, corporate actions to uphold commitments are associated with a conservatively estimated 10 percent net reduction in flaring in Africa without a corresponding reduction in oil production or local economic activity in extraction communities. Our findings suggest that environmental commitments are backed by corporate policies akin to establishing a uniform cost of pollution across the firm’s global operations and therefore may alleviate the problems posed by globally fragmented regulation.
                  Data Availability: All data except for Enverus oil and gas are publicly available. Enverus is available for purchase on a subscription basis.
                  JEL Classifications: F18; K23; K32; L71; M14; M48; N57; O13; Q35; Q52; Q53; Q56.
